node.label: Donna Haraway
node.date_label: Manifesto for Cyborgs (1985) · Situated Knowledges (1988) · Primate Visions (1989) · Staying with the Trouble (2016)
node.description: In “Situated Knowledges” (1988), Donna Haraway argued that objectivity requires accountable, embodied perspectives. Her “Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985; collected in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women, 1991) used the human-machine figure to challenge fixed divisions between nature, culture and technology. Primate Visions (1989) made race and gender part of the historical explanation of primatology. Louise Barrett (2017) recalls gaining a new perspective from that book while recording Matt Cartmill’s hostile 1991 response to its writing. Haraway’s later companion-species work asks what humans can learn through relations with other organisms. In When Species Meet (2008), she criticizes Derrida’s response to his cat and Deleuze and Guattari’s becoming-animal, as Perry Zurn and Marie Draz respectively read her. Zurn (2018) accepts her objection to Derrida’s cat encounter but argues that deconstruction remains curious at the level of texts. “Making Kin” (2015) and Staying with the Trouble (2016) extend her account of interdependence into ecological crisis and the possibilities of living together on a damaged earth.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “A Manifesto for Cyborgs” (1985); “Situated Knowledges” (1988); Primate Visions (1989); Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991, collection); The Companion Species Manifesto (2003); When Species Meet (2008 bibliographic year; publisher release 2007); Staying with the Trouble (2016).
node.scope_note: Selected pages of Situated Knowledges and the primary Making Kin essay were read, with exact scopes in the source notes. Primate Visions and When Species Meet are represented through named readers and publisher descriptions. Manifesto and other book bodies, Derrida’s and Deleuze/Guattari’s originals, and the full Harvey–Haraway exchange remain unread. Zurn was read only on pp. 84–90 and Barrett only in the publisher’s opening extract.

proposed_edges.relationship: In When Species Meet (2008), Haraway faults Derrida’s failure to pursue curiosity about his cat, as Zurn (2018) reads her.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Zurn p. 87, paragraph beginning In one sense and its continuation, reports Haraway’s admiration and specific objection; Berkowitz p. 8 n. 15 quotes When Species Meet p. 20 (discussion pp. 19–27). Haraway’s and Derrida’s originals unread. This concerns a particular encounter, not rejection of all deconstruction.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Marie Draz reports, When Species Meet (2008) criticizes Deleuze and Guattari’s becoming-animal within a challenge to wild/domestic boundaries.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Signed review reproduced under Praise, paragraph beginning Of particular interest: “critiques of Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari”. Complete review read; original book passage unread and its print pages unverified. Joint authorship retained; Guattari has no eligible endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: Situated Knowledges (1988) develops embodied, accountable objectivity for feminist science studies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Carried forward from existing graph source haraway_situated. Its verification, checked 2026-09-10, records consultation of the journal text, pp. 575–577 and 582–585, for situated objectivity, accountability and rejection of relativism, without implying a universal feminist position. The edge uses the latter pages. This correction read the existing source record; it did not re-read the article. The DOI resolved to a journal landing page without readable article text. The individual contribution complements gender → sts edge_337.

proposed_edges.relationship: Primate Visions (1989) examines race and gender in primatology’s history, as Barrett (2017) describes it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Barrett’s publisher extract, p. 309, paragraph beginning That book: identifies a historical account of primatology. Foundation biography, paragraphs beginning She gained and For instance, independently describes race/gender analysis. Book unread; 1989 original year from UCSC bibliography, not foundation’s 1990.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Making Kin (2015), Haraway treats environmental change as the historically situated work of human and nonhuman assemblages.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary HTML, opening two paragraphs and note 5: “assemblages of organic species and of abiotic actors make history”. Read argument linking historical differences, ecological change and plantation labour; this is an interdisciplinary contribution to environmental explanation, not a claim to found environmental history.

proposed_edges.relationship: In How to Talk About the Body? The Normative Dimension of Science Studies (2004), Bruno Latour takes up Haraway’s call to locate political struggles within the sciences rather than leave scientific authority untouched while restricting activism to subjective feelings.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the author-posted journal article’s opening and concluding argument, especially pp. 226–227. Latour explicitly aligns his intervention with Haraway’s advocacy; he does not identify a particular Haraway publication here. This supports a specific conceptual uptake, not a claim that his entire account of bodies originated with her.
